title: Version Control (Git)
description: The Git you use every day: committing, branching, integrating, undoing and collaborating.
resumo: Flow: `git add` (staging), `git commit` (local history), `git push` (remote). A commit is local until you push.
`git fetch` downloads without merging; `git pull` = fetch + merge (or `--rebase`).
One short branch per task, merged through a reviewed pull request.
Merge keeps the history; rebase makes it linear but rewrites commits — never on a shared branch.
Before committing: `git diff` (not staged) and `git diff --staged` (going into the commit).
Undo: `git revert` adds a reverse commit (safe); `reset --soft/--mixed/--hard` only for commits not pushed.
`git stash -u` puts work aside; `.gitignore` does not affect files already tracked (`git rm --cached`).
Conventional Commits (`feat:`, `fix:`) and SemVer tags (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH); `git push` does not push tags.

subsections.subtitle: What Is Git?
subsections.description: A distributed history of every change to the code.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** code shared by zip file or email: no history, files named "final_v2_real.zip", and two people overwriting each other's work.

**Concept:** Git is a distributed version control system: every clone has the full history. A commit is a snapshot of the project with an author, a date, a message and a pointer to its parent commit. Your work moves through three areas: the working directory (your files), the staging area or index (what goes into the next commit) and the repository (the history, in `.git`). A remote such as `origin` on GitHub is just another copy of the repository.

**How it works:** you change files, choose what to stage with `git add`, record it with `git commit`, and share it with `git push`.
examples.code:
working directory --git add--> staging area --git commit--> local repository --git push--> remote (origin)
                                                                     <--git fetch / git pull--

git init                                   # new repository in the current folder
git config --global user.name "Ana Silva"
git config --global user.email "ana@example.com"
git status                                 # what changed, what is staged
examples.interview_question: What is Git, and what are the working directory, the staging area and the repository?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Thinking `git commit` shares or backs up your work. A commit is local until you push it; if your laptop breaks before that, it is gone.
examples.code:
git commit -m "fix: correct the tax rate"
# the laptop breaks: the fix is lost — the commit existed only here

git push          # now it is on the remote

subsections.subtitle: Basic Workflow: Clone, Commit and Push
subsections.formerSubtitle: Fluxo Básico: Clone, Commit e Push
subsections.description: Getting a project, changing it and sending the change back.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** you need the team's project on your machine, make a change, and send it back without breaking anyone's work.

**Concept:** `git clone` copies a remote repository, history included. `git add` stages changes, `git commit` records them with a message, `git push` sends your commits to the remote, and `git pull` brings in other people's commits.

**How it works:** commit small, one logical change at a time, with a message that says what and why. Push only commits: without a new commit, `git push` answers "Everything up-to-date".
examples.code:
git clone https://github.com/shop/api.git
cd api
# ... edit files ...
git status                            # see what changed
git add src/OrderService.java         # stage it
git commit -m "feat: add order cancellation"
git push origin main                  # send it to the remote
git log --oneline -3                  # the latest commits
examples.interview_question: What is the basic Git workflow, from clone to push?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: `git add .` without looking. It stages everything — passwords in `.env`, build output, IDE files — and they go into the history. Check `git status` and `git diff --staged` first.
examples.code:
# WRONG
git add .
git commit -m "feat: add login"
# also committed: .env with passwords, target/, .idea/

# RIGHT: look before you commit
git status
git diff --staged
git restore --staged .env        # unstage what should not go in

subsections.subtitle: Branches and Merging
subsections.description: Parallel lines of work, brought back together.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** you are building a feature for a week while a production bug has to be fixed today — in the same code.

**Concept:** a branch is a movable pointer to a commit; creating one is instant. `HEAD` marks where you are. Merging integrates one branch into another: a fast-forward if the target did not move, otherwise a merge commit with two parents. A conflict happens when both sides changed the same lines.

**How it works:** to resolve a conflict, edit the file, keep the right version (or combine both), remove the markers, then `git add` and `git commit`. Run the tests afterwards: a merge without textual conflicts can still break the logic.
examples.code:
git switch -c feature/discount      # create and switch to a new branch
# ... commits ...
git switch main
git merge feature/discount          # integrate

# A conflict looks like this in the file:
<<<<<<< HEAD
price = 10;
=======
price = 12;
>>>>>>> feature/discount

# edit, keep the right line, remove the markers, then:
git add Price.java
git commit
examples.interview_question: How do you resolve a merge conflict?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Committing the conflict markers. The file no longer compiles, or worse, a config file is silently wrong. `git diff --check` catches leftover markers before you commit.
examples.code:
git add .
git diff --cached --check
# Price.java:12: leftover conflict marker
# -> fix the file before committing

subsections.subtitle: Merge vs Rebase
subsections.description: Two ways to bring main's changes into your branch.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** main moved on while you worked on your branch. You need its changes — and there are two ways to get them, with different histories.

**Concept:** merge keeps the history as it happened and adds a merge commit with two parents. Rebase replays your commits on top of the latest main, giving a straight line — but it creates new commits with new hashes, which rewrites history.

**How it works:** the golden rule: never rebase commits that other people already have. Rebasing your own branch is fine; if it was already pushed, update it with `git push --force-with-lease`, which refuses to overwrite commits you have not seen.
examples.code:
Before:                  A---B---C  main
                              \
                               D---E  feature

Merge main into feature:  A---B---C-------M  feature    (M has two parents)
                              \         /
                               D-------E

Rebase feature onto main: A---B---C---D'---E'  feature  (D', E' are new commits)

# Option A: merge
git switch feature
git merge main

# Option B: rebase
git switch feature
git rebase main
examples.interview_question: What is the difference between merge and rebase, and when can rebase cause problems?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Rebasing a shared branch and force-pushing it. Everyone who already pulled it now has a history that no longer exists on the remote, and commits can be lost when they sync.
examples.code:
# WRONG: rewriting main, which everybody has
git switch main
git rebase -i HEAD~5
git push --force

# RIGHT: rebase only your own branch, and force with lease
git switch feature/login
git rebase main
git push --force-with-lease

subsections.subtitle: Fetch and Pull
subsections.description: Getting other people's commits — with or without merging.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** teammates pushed while you worked. You need their changes, and you may want to see them before mixing them with yours.

**Concept:** `git fetch` downloads new commits and updates the remote-tracking branches (`origin/main`) without touching your files. `git pull` is `git fetch` followed by a merge — or a rebase, with `--rebase` — into your current branch.

**How it works:** fetch first when you want to inspect what changed. `git pull --rebase` replays your local commits on top of the remote ones and avoids small merge commits; `pull.rebase true` makes it the default.
examples.code:
git fetch origin
git log --oneline HEAD..origin/main     # remote commits you do not have yet
git diff HEAD origin/main               # what they change
git merge origin/main                   # integrate when ready

git pull --rebase                       # fetch + replay your commits on top
git config --global pull.rebase true    # make it the default
examples.interview_question: When would you use git fetch instead of git pull?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Pulling with uncommitted changes in files that the incoming commits also change. Git refuses, to protect your work. Commit or stash first.
examples.code:
git pull
# error: Your local changes to the following files would be overwritten by merge:
#   src/OrderService.java
# Please commit your changes or stash them before you merge.

# RIGHT
git stash
git pull
git stash pop

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** build output, logs, IDE settings and an `.env` file with passwords end up in the repository.

**Concept:** `.gitignore` lists patterns of files Git should not track: `*.log`, `target/`, `.env`, `.idea/`. `*` is a wildcard, a trailing `/` means a directory, a leading `/` means only at the root, and `!` makes an exception. It only applies to files that are not tracked yet.

**How it works:** create it when the project starts (GitHub has templates per language) and commit it. `git check-ignore -v` tells you which rule ignores a file.
examples.code:
# .gitignore for a Java/Maven project
target/
*.log
.env
.idea/
*.iml
.vscode/
!.vscode/settings.json      # exception: keep this one

# Which rule ignores this file?
git check-ignore -v target/app.jar
examples.interview_question: What happens if a file that is already tracked is added to .gitignore?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Adding an already tracked file to `.gitignore` and expecting Git to forget it. It stays tracked. Remove it from the index with `git rm --cached` (the file stays on disk). If it was a secret, it is still in the history: change the password.
examples.code:
# Content of .gitignore
.env

# Terminal
git rm --cached .env      # stop tracking a file that was already committed
git add .gitignore
git commit -m "chore: stop tracking .env"

subsections.subtitle: Status, Diff and Restore
subsections.description: Seeing exactly what changed, and undoing local changes.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** before committing you need to know exactly what changed — and sometimes you want to throw an experiment away.

**Concept:** `git status` lists modified, staged and untracked files. `git diff` shows changes in the working directory that are not staged yet; `git diff --staged` shows what is staged and will go into the next commit. `git restore --staged` unstages a file and keeps the change; `git restore` discards the change.

**How it works:** review both diffs before every commit. `git status -s` gives a short view: `M` modified, `A` added, `??` untracked.
examples.code:
git status -s                     # short view
git diff                          # changes not staged yet
git diff --staged                 # what goes into the next commit
git restore --staged Order.java   # unstage, keep the change
git restore Order.java            # discard the local change
examples.interview_question: How do you use git diff to review changes before a commit?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Discarding work you might still want. `git restore` on uncommitted changes cannot be undone — they were never committed, so the reflog cannot bring them back. When in doubt, stash instead.
examples.code:
# WRONG: uncommitted work is gone for good
git restore .

# RIGHT when unsure: put it aside
git stash push -m "experiment with the new tax rule"

subsections.subtitle: Revert and Reset
subsections.description: Undoing commits — safely on shared branches, or locally.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a bad commit went in. It may already be pushed, or it may exist only on your machine — and the right way to undo it differs.

**Concept:** `git revert` creates a new commit that undoes a previous one; history is kept, so it is safe on shared branches. `git reset` moves the branch back to an earlier commit: `--soft` keeps the changes staged, `--mixed` (the default) keeps them unstaged, and `--hard` deletes them. Reset rewrites history, so use it only on commits that were not pushed.

**How it works:** pushed commit: revert. Local commit you want to redo: reset `--soft` or `--mixed`. `--hard` only when you really want to throw the changes away.
examples.code:
git revert HEAD            # a new commit that undoes the last one
git reset --soft HEAD~1    # undo the commit; changes stay staged
git reset HEAD~1           # --mixed (default): changes stay, unstaged
git reset --hard HEAD~1    # undo the commit AND discard the changes
examples.interview_question: What is the difference between git revert and git reset, and between reset --soft and --hard?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Undoing a pushed commit with reset and force push. Everyone who pulled it now has a commit that no longer exists on the remote. On shared branches, revert.
examples.code:
# WRONG
git reset --hard HEAD~1
git push --force

# RIGHT
git revert a1b2c3d
git push

subsections.subtitle: Git Stash
subsections.description: Putting unfinished work aside for a moment.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** you are halfway through a change when an urgent bug on main needs fixing. Half-done work should not be committed, and switching branches would carry it along — or be refused.

**Concept:** `git stash` saves your uncommitted changes (staged and unstaged) on a stack and cleans the working directory. `git stash pop` brings them back and removes the entry; `git stash apply` brings them back and keeps it.

**How it works:** give each stash a message, so `git stash list` tells you what is what. Stashes are local and easy to forget — do not use them as long-term storage.
examples.code:
git stash push -m "half-done discount screen"
git switch main
# ... fix the bug, commit, push ...
git switch feature/discount
git stash list           # stash@{0}: On feature/discount: half-done discount screen
git stash pop            # changes are back, entry removed
examples.interview_question: How does git stash help when you have to switch tasks?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Expecting new files to be stashed. By default, untracked files stay in the working directory and follow you to the other branch. Add `-u`.
examples.code:
git stash
git switch main
git status          # NewFile.java is still here: untracked files are not stashed

# RIGHT
git stash push -u -m "wip"

subsections.subtitle: Log and Blame
subsections.description: Who changed a line, when, and why.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a line looks wrong. Who changed it, when, and why?

**Concept:** `git log` shows the history: `--oneline` for a short view, `--graph` for branches, `-p` for the changes, `-S "text"` for commits that added or removed a piece of text, `-- path` for one file. `git blame` shows, for every line, the last commit that changed it. `git show <hash>` displays that commit's message and diff.

**How it works:** blame finds the commit; the commit message and its pull request explain the why. That is a big reason to write good commit messages.
examples.code:
git log --oneline --graph --all           # history as a graph
git log -p -- src/TaxService.java         # every change to one file
git log -S "TAX_RATE"                     # commits that added or removed this text
git blame -L 40,60 src/TaxService.java    # who last changed lines 40-60
git show 3f9a2b1                          # the full commit: message + diff
examples.interview_question: How do you use git log and git blame to investigate a bug?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Trusting blame after a mass reformat or file move. Every line shows the formatting commit, not the real origin. Ignore whitespace, follow moved lines, and list reformat commits in an ignore file.
examples.code:
git blame src/TaxService.java   # every line: "style: reformat code"

# RIGHT
git blame -w -M -C src/TaxService.java                  # ignore whitespace, follow moved lines
git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs  # skip known reformat commits

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** code that goes straight to main without anyone looking brings bugs, inconsistent style, and knowledge stuck in one person's head.

**Concept:** a pull request (a merge request in GitLab) proposes merging a branch. It shows the diff, runs CI, and lets reviewers comment and approve before the merge. It can be merged with a merge commit, squashed into one commit, or rebased.

**How it works:** keep a PR small and about one subject, with a description of what changes, why, and how it was tested. Push fixes to the same branch; the PR updates itself.
examples.code:
git switch -c feature/cancel-order
git commit -m "feat(orders): allow cancelling unpaid orders"
git push -u origin feature/cancel-order
# open the PR on GitHub (or: gh pr create --fill)
# CI runs, reviewers comment -> push more commits to the same branch
# approved + CI green -> merge (squash), delete the branch
git switch main && git pull
examples.interview_question: Why are pull requests important in team projects?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: A huge PR with several subjects. Nobody can review 3,000 lines properly, so it gets approved without real review. Split it into PRs that each do one thing.
examples.code:
WRONG: one PR "various changes" — 48 files, +3,200 lines:
       new feature + refactor + dependency upgrade

RIGHT: three PRs
  1. chore(deps): upgrade jackson to 2.17.2
  2. refactor(orders): extract PriceCalculator
  3. feat(orders): allow cancelling unpaid orders

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a history full of "fix", "wip" and "changes" says nothing. Finding when a feature arrived, or writing release notes, means reading every diff.

**Concept:** Conventional Commits uses the format `type(scope): description`. Common types: `feat` (new feature), `fix` (bug fix), `refactor`, `test`, `docs`, `chore`, `ci`. The subject is short and imperative; the body explains why. A breaking change is marked with `!` or a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer.

**How it works:** tools read these messages to generate changelogs and choose the next version automatically: `feat` → minor, `fix` → patch, breaking change → major.
examples.code:
git commit -m "feat(orders): add order cancellation"
git commit -m "fix(auth): correct JWT token expiry"
git commit -m "refactor: extract shipping calculation into a Strategy"

# Breaking change
git commit -m "feat(api)!: remove the /v1/users endpoint" -m "BREAKING CHANGE: use /v2/users"
examples.interview_question: How do you write good commit messages?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Messages that only say what changed in the code, not why. The diff already shows what; the message is the only place for the reason.
examples.code:
# WRONG
git commit -m "fix"
git commit -m "change timeout to 5s"

# RIGHT
git commit -m "fix(payment): raise gateway timeout to 5s" \
           -m "The gateway takes up to 4s at peak; 2s caused failed payments."

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** "which code is running in production?" With no marks in the history, nobody can answer quickly — or roll back to the previous release.

**Concept:** a tag is a fixed name for a commit, usually a release. Annotated tags (`-a`) store author, date and message, and are the recommended kind. Semantic Versioning (`MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`) tells users the impact: MAJOR for incompatible changes, MINOR for compatible features, PATCH for fixes.

**How it works:** CI/CD pipelines often build and publish a release when a `v*` tag is pushed. Checking out a tag puts you in "detached HEAD" — fine for looking around; create a branch if you need to change something.
examples.code:
git tag -a v1.4.0 -m "Release 1.4.0: order cancellation"
git push origin v1.4.0

git tag --list "v1.*"       # list tags
git checkout v1.3.2         # inspect an old version (detached HEAD)
examples.interview_question: How do you version releases with tags in Git?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Forgetting that `git push` does not push tags. The tag exists only on your machine, and the release pipeline never starts. Push the tag itself, or use `--follow-tags`.
examples.code:
git tag -a v1.4.0 -m "Release 1.4.0"
git push                  # pushes commits, NOT tags

# RIGHT
git push origin v1.4.0    # or: git push --follow-tags
